In Class 4B of the municipal school in Pune, Ramesh sir noticed that Naveen knew almost every answer and shouted most of them first. He tapped his pencil, tipped his chair and was out of his seat six times in one maths period.
Some staff-room voices called him a menace. Ramesh sir didn't. Instead he moved Naveen near the window, made him the board cleaner so he could get up between lessons, and gave him a small card to hold up instead of calling out.
Things improved, but not completely. So at the parent meeting he spoke to Naveen's mother gently. 'He's bright and trying hard. If you think it would help, the school counsellor can suggest where to get a proper assessment. It's only to understand him better.'

qa.q: What job did Ramesh sir give Naveen?
qa.a: Board cleaner, so he could get up between lessons.

qa.q: How did Ramesh sir feel about Naveen, unlike some staff-room voices?
qa.a: He felt patient and hopeful about Naveen, seeing him as bright and trying hard rather than a menace.

qa.q: What choice did Ramesh sir make when things improved but not completely?
qa.a: He gently raised with Naveen's mother that the school counsellor could suggest where to get a proper assessment, only to understand Naveen better.

qa.q: How might Naveen's mother feel hearing her son called bright and trying hard?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and less defensive, and more open to an assessment because it came with respect, not blame.

grounding: Shows a teacher who sees a bright, restless pupil, adjusts seating and gives movement breaks instead of labelling, and gently suggests a professional assessment.

'Seven eights are fifty-six!' Divyansh shouted before Hansa Ma'am had finished the question.
'Right, Divyansh. Next time, hand up first. Can you try?'
'Sorry, Ma'am. It just jumps out.'
Ten minutes later he was standing by the window. 'Ma'am, can I sharpen my pencil?'
'You've sharpened it twice already.' She smiled. 'Tell you what. Be my messenger. Take this note to the office and back. Then sit and finish four sums.'
'Really?' He was already at the door.
When he came back, he finished all four sums, fast.
At home time Hansa Ma'am said, 'Divyansh, I'd like to talk to your Papa tomorrow. Nothing bad. Just how to help you learn best, maybe with advice from someone trained in this.'
'Am I in trouble?'
'No. You're clever. I want to help.'

qa.q: What answer did Divyansh shout out?
qa.a: Seven eights are fifty-six.

qa.q: How does Hansa Ma'am feel about Divyansh's blurting and restlessness?
qa.a: She feels patient and caring rather than annoyed; she smiles, makes him her messenger and wants to help him learn best.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa Ma'am make when Divyansh was out of his seat again?
qa.a: She made him her messenger to the office, giving him a movement break, and afterwards he finished four sums fast.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Hansa Ma'am says 'You're clever. I want to help'?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and trusted, since he was afraid he was in trouble.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a bright pupil who blurts and cannot sit still, giving movement breaks rather than labels, and planning to talk with the family about expert advice.

passage: In my first year teaching Class 4, I nearly got Sachin completely wrong. I'm Jatin, and on the second day I wrote "disruptive" in my notebook. He was out of his seat every ten minutes and shouted answers before I finished the question. But the answers were right, almost always. So I tried a few things. I moved him to the front, near the door, and made him board monitor, so he could get up and wipe the board between lessons. I gave him a soft ball to squeeze. He settled a little. Then I asked his parents to come in. I didn't use any labels. I just told them what I'd seen, and that a child specialist could help us understand him better, if they felt it was needed.

qa.q: What job did Jatin give Sachin?
qa.a: Board monitor.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel about Sachin at first, and later?
qa.a: Jatin first felt irritated, writing "disruptive", then became curious and hopeful on noticing Sachin's answers were almost always right.

qa.q: What did Jatin do instead of labelling Sachin?
qa.a: Changed the seating, gave movement jobs and a ball to squeeze, and talked with the parents about a specialist if needed.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel being made board monitor?
qa.a: Sachin probably feels trusted and relieved to have a reason to move.

grounding: Shows a teacher who first labels a restless, bright pupil, then adjusts seating, adds movement and talks with the family.

passage:
Class 3 note, Wednesday. Santosh knew the answer to every question in science today and shouted each one before anyone else could think. He was out of his seat six times and drummed on the desk through reading. He is bright and curious, and I can see how hard he tries to sit still. I have moved him to the front corner, away from the window, and given him two errands each lesson: carrying books to the office and sharpening pencils. He was calmer after each one. I have asked his parents to meet me on Friday to share what I have noticed, and to talk about whether a professional assessment might help us support him.
Kishore

qa.q: How many times was Santosh out of his seat?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: How does Kishore seem to feel about Santosh?
qa.a: Kishore seems caring and patient, seeing a bright, curious child who is trying hard.

qa.q: What changes did Kishore make, and why might they help?
qa.a: A front-corner seat and two errands per lesson, which give Santosh movement and fewer distractions.

qa.q: How might Santosh's parents feel about the Friday meeting?
qa.a: They may feel nervous but reassured, since Kishore shares observations without labelling their son.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher noticing a bright, restless pupil and adjusting seating and movement before talking with the family.

passage:
Tuesday night. Kunal again today. He blurted the answer to the fraction sum before I'd finished writing it, and got it right. Then he fell off his chair. Twice. The class laughed. Honestly, I felt irritated, and then guilty, because I've seen his face when he's told off. He really does try. So tomorrow: a new seat near my desk, not by the window. A wiggle break for the whole class every twenty minutes, so he isn't singled out. And I've written to his parents asking to meet. I don't want to put a name on anything. I just want to tell them what I see, and ask whether they'd like to talk to the school counsellor about getting him properly assessed.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How often will the wiggle break happen?
qa.a: Every twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel after Kunal fell off his chair?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt irritated at first, then guilty, knowing Kunal really tries.

qa.q: Why is a whole-class wiggle break a thoughtful choice?
qa.a: It gives Kunal movement without singling him out in front of classmates.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when the class laughs?
qa.a: Kunal is probably embarrassed, even while trying to join in.

grounding: Shows a teacher who notices a restless pupil, adjusts seating and breaks, and plans to talk with his family about an assessment.

passage:
In the one-room school near Kheda, Baljeet Sir noticed that Dilnaz knew every answer before he finished the question. She shouted them out, bounced on the bench, and dropped her slate twice an hour.
Some teachers would have called her naughty. Baljeet Sir watched for a week instead. When she had a job, she was fine.
So he moved her to the front near the door. Every half hour she carried the chalk box to the next room or rang the hand bell. He gave her a small card: "Hand up, count three."
Her blurting halved. On market day he met her Abba by the cloth stall. "She is very bright," he said. "Sitting still is hard for her. If it keeps troubling her, the doctor at the district hospital could advise you." Abba nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet Sir move Dilnaz?
qa.a: He moved her to the front near the door.

qa.q: What was Baljeet Sir thinking and feeling when he chose to watch for a week?
qa.a: He felt curious and patient, not annoyed; he wanted to understand Dilnaz rather than label her naughty.

qa.q: Which of Baljeet Sir's changes worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving her movement jobs and the "hand up, count three" card helped, because they gave her body a way to move and a clear signal to wait.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz when she gets to carry the chalk box or ring the bell?
qa.a: She probably feels trusted and relieved to move, and afterwards it is easier for her to wait her turn.

grounding: Baljeet Sir notices a bright, restless pupil, adjusts her seating and gives movement breaks instead of labelling, and talks with her father about seeking advice.
